name: Design Patterns and SOLID
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: SOLID, composition over inheritance and the patterns interns meet: strategy, factory, observer, adapter, decorator, DI and MVC.

lesson.intro: Design patterns are named, reusable answers to recurring problems: swapping an algorithm, reacting to events, wrapping a vendor SDK, keeping dependencies testable. You will meet them in every codebase and hear them in reviews and interviews. This lesson covers the principles and the patterns interns meet.
objectives: Explain each SOLID principle through the problem it prevents
Choose composition over inheritance, and know when inheritance still fits
Match a problem to strategy, factory, observer, adapter or decorator
Replace singletons with dependency injection to make code testable
Keep business rules out of controllers in an MVC app

sections.title: SOLID in five small examples
sections.key: SOLID describes code that is easy to change: one job, extend without editing, honest subclasses, small interfaces, and depending on abstractions rather than concrete classes.
sections.body:
Five principles, gathered by Robert C. Martin and named SOLID by Michael Feathers, describe code that stays easy to change. You hear them in reviews and interviews ("how would you make this extensible?"), and each is easiest to grasp through the problem it prevents:

[[visual]]

In Python the "interface" is often implicit (duck typing) or written as a `typing.Protocol` or abstract base class; in TypeScript it is an `interface`. Either way, code depends on what an object can do, not on which class it is.

[[code]]

SOLID is a set of forces to weigh, not commandments. Applied mechanically, it turns a 50-line script into a dozen one-method classes. Apply it where change actually happens.

visual.title: SOLID
rows: S: Single responsibility
One reason to change
A `Report` that computes totals, renders HTML and emails itself
A calculator, a renderer and a mailer
O: Open/closed
Add behavior by adding code, not by editing code that works
Adding a shape means editing an `if shape.kind == ...` chain in five functions
Each shape has its own `area()`; a new `Hexagon` touches nothing else
L: Liskov substitution
A subclass works anywhere its parent is expected, with no surprises
`ReadOnlyFile(File)` raises on `write()`; `Square(Rectangle)` breaks code that sets width and height separately
Do not force the subclass; share a smaller interface instead
I: Interface segregation
Do not make clients depend on methods they do not use
A `Machine` interface forces a basic printer to implement `scan()` and `fax()`
Small interfaces: `Printer`, `Scanner`
D: Dependency inversion
High-level policy depends on abstractions, not details
`SignupService` builds its own `SmtpClient`
Depend on "something that can send email" and pass it in: another provider, or a fake in tests

sections.pitfall: Applying SOLID mechanically: an interface, a factory and three classes for logic with one implementation that never changes. Add the abstraction when a second implementation, or a test needing a fake, shows up.

check.question: `ReadOnlyFile` subclasses `File` and raises an error in `write()`. Code that accepts any `File` and writes to it now crashes. Which principle is broken?
choices: Single responsibility
Liskov substitution
Interface segregation
Open/closed
check.explanation: Callers were promised that any File can be written to. A subclass that refuses cannot stand in for its parent. Often the fix is a different hierarchy, such as separate Readable and Writable interfaces.

sections.title: Composition over inheritance
sections.key: Favor composition (an object holds parts and delegates) over inheritance; keep inheritance for true is-a relationships that honor the parent's contract.
sections.body:
A notifications module starts with `Notifier`, `EmailNotifier` and `SmsNotifier`. Then product wants logged emails, SMS with retries, logged SMS with retries. Every combination needs another subclass, and a change to `Notifier` ripples through all of them: a **class explosion**.

[[visual]]

**Inheritance** models "is-a" and shares code by extending a parent. **Composition** models "has-a": an object holds others and delegates to them. "Favor object composition over class inheritance" comes from the 1994 Gang of Four book, Design Patterns.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

Frameworks often ask you to subclass their base classes, and that is fine. Keep your own hierarchies to one or two levels, and reach for composition when a class name needs two "ands".

items.title: Inheritance: is-a
points: One subclass per combination of behaviors
A subclass depends on its parent's internals, so a harmless parent change can break it (the fragile base class problem)
Right for true is-a that honors the contract: `InsufficientFundsError(Exception)`, a Django model, a `unittest.TestCase`

items.title: Composition: has-a
points: Mix and match: `Notifier(channels=[email, sms], logger=log)` covers every combination
Depends only on collaborators' public methods
Tests pass a fake channel to the constructor
Construction says exactly what you get

sections.pitfall: Inheriting just to reuse a few helpers, as in `class OrderService(DatabaseHelper)` or `class Stack(list)`. If the child is not truly a kind of the parent, hold the helper as an attribute instead.

check.question: `class Stack(list)` subclasses Python's list to reuse append and pop. What is the main problem?
choices: Built-in types cannot be subclassed in Python
It makes push and pop slower than a plain list
It violates DRY
Callers inherit every list method, so they can insert in the middle or sort it; holding a list privately exposes only stack operations
check.explanation: A stack is not a list: it promises last-in, first-out access. Inheriting exposes insert, sort, slicing and more, all of which break that promise. Composition (a private list inside) exposes exactly push, pop and peek.

sections.title: Strategy and factory
sections.key: Strategy puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so callers never change; a factory decides in one place which one to build.
sections.body:
Checkout needs a shipping cost: standard, express, and as of this sprint free shipping for members. Version one is an `if` chain inside `checkout()`: every new option edits checkout, and testing one rule runs all of it.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

You meet factories constantly, often without the name: `logging.getLogger(name)`, alternative constructors such as `datetime.fromisoformat(text)` (a `@classmethod` in Python), and `document.createElement('div')`.

The signal in code review: the same `if`/`elif` on a type or kind string repeated in several functions. That is a strategy waiting to be extracted, plus a factory to pick it.

items.title: Strategy
points: Each interchangeable algorithm sits behind one interface
Checkout just asks: `shipping.cost(cart_total)`
A new rule is a new strategy and checkout does not change: open/closed in action
One operation with no configuration or state? In Python just pass a function, like the `key` for `sorted()`
TypeScript: `interface ShippingStrategy { cost(total: number): number }`

items.title: Factory
points: Decides in one place which object to create
`make_shipping("express")` returns the right strategy
A dict from names to classes keeps it one lookup
Normalize the input; an unknown name raises one clear error, never a silent fallback
Callers depend only on the interface

sections.pitfall: Building a strategy hierarchy for a choice that has one implementation and no sign of a second. A plain function is enough until a second variant really appears.

activity.title: Add a strategy without touching checkout
activity.prompt: Run it: the factory rejects "member". Add a MemberShipping class with a cost() method that returns 0, and register it in SHIPPING_OPTIONS. Notice that checkout_total never changes: adding behavior meant adding code, not editing working code.

props.task: Make the output: standard: 45, express: 55, member: 40 (one per line)

check.question: The same `if payment_type == "card" ... elif payment_type == "paypal"` chain appears in four functions. What does it most suggest?
choices: Convert each chain into a nested ternary expression
Move all four functions into one long function
One strategy per payment type behind a shared interface, chosen by a factory
Make payment_type a global variable
check.explanation: Repeated type checks mean the knowledge about each payment type is scattered. Strategies gather it into one class per type, and a factory makes the choice once. Adding a new type then means adding a class, not editing four functions.

sections.title: Observer and pub/sub
sections.key: Observer lets a subject notify its subscribed listeners; pub/sub adds a broker so publishers and subscribers know only a topic, not each other. Always unsubscribe.
sections.body:
When an order ships, the system emails the customer, updates analytics and refreshes the warehouse dashboard. If `ship_order()` calls all three, shipping depends on email, analytics and the dashboard, and every new reaction edits it.

The **observer pattern** flips that dependency. The **subject** keeps a list of **observers** (listeners) and notifies each one when something happens. You already use it: `button.addEventListener('click', handler)`, Node's `emitter.on('shipped', fn)`, and UI frameworks that re-render components subscribed to state.

**Publish/subscribe** (pub/sub) puts a **broker** in the middle:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

[[visual 3]]

items.title: Observer
points: The subject holds direct references to its listeners
Usually inside one process
DOM events, Node `EventEmitter`, UI state

items.title: Pub/sub
points: Publishers send to a named topic, not knowing who listens, or whether anyone does
Subscribers listen to topics, not knowing who publishes
In one process: an event bus. Between services: Redis pub/sub, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ, Kafka

messages.note: The order service knows only the topic

visual.title: Costs to keep in mind
rows: Hidden control flow: `publish('shipped')` does not show what runs
Keep event names explicit and listeners easy to find
Leaks: a listener never removed keeps firing and keeps its objects alive
Pair every subscribe with an unsubscribe; in React, return a cleanup from `useEffect`
In a naive loop, one listener that throws stops the rest
Decide whether to catch per listener
Ordering
Never let listeners depend on running in a particular order

sections.pitfall: Subscribing from an object or component that is later thrown away, and never unsubscribing. The listener keeps firing and keeps the object in memory. Keep the unsubscribe function and call it during cleanup.

activity.title: Add a listener, remove a listener
activity.prompt: Replace TODO 1 with a subscription that logs warehouse: pack order and the id, and replace TODO 2 with a call that stops analytics. Notice that shipOrder never changes: the subject does not know who is listening.

props.task: Make order 2 notify email and the warehouse, but not analytics.
props.expectOutput:
email: order 1 shipped
analytics: order 1
email: order 2 shipped
warehouse: pack order 2

check.question: What is the key difference between the classic observer pattern and pub/sub through a broker?
choices: Observers can only be used in browsers
Pub/sub requires listeners to run in a fixed order
The observer pattern cannot pass data with an event
With pub/sub, publishers and subscribers know only a topic, not each other
check.explanation: An observer's subject holds references to its listeners. A broker removes even that: publishers send to a topic and subscribers read from it, so either side can be added, removed or scaled without the other noticing.

sections.title: Adapter and decorator
sections.key: An adapter translates a foreign interface into yours; a decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior, so decorators stack.
sections.body:
Your app charges cards through its own small interface, `charge(amount_cents, customer_id)`. Then the company switches to a provider whose SDK wants `create_payment(amount={...}, payer=...)`. Rather than rewriting every call site, you write an **adapter**: a class that implements your interface and translates each call. The next switch is one new adapter.

A **decorator** (the design pattern) also wraps an object, but keeps the **same interface** and **adds behavior**: logging, caching, timing, retries. Because the wrapper looks like what it wraps, you can stack them.

[[visual]]

A **Python decorator**, the `@something` line above a function, applies the idea to functions: it takes a function and returns a wrapped one. `@functools.lru_cache` adds caching, FastAPI's `@app.get("/users")` registers a route, and you can write your own `@timed`.

[[code]]

items.title: Adapter
points: A different interface comes out than goes in: it translates
Wraps a vendor SDK, a legacy module, or an API whose fields differ (`user_name` versus `username`)
Vendor code lives in one place: one small seam to fake in tests

items.title: Decorator
points: The same interface comes out as goes in: it adds behavior
Logging, caching, timing, retries, permission checks
Stackable: `LoggingGateway(AcmePayAdapter(client), log)`

sections.tip: In your own Python decorators, call `func(*args, **kwargs)`, return its result, and add `@functools.wraps(func)` so the wrapped function keeps its name and docstring.
sections.pitfall: Letting the vendor's types leak past the adapter, such as passing the SDK's response objects around the app. Switching providers then means editing every file again. Translate at the boundary.

check.question: You wrap a cache client so every `get` and `set` call is timed and logged, keeping exactly the same methods. Which pattern is that?
choices: Adapter
Decorator
Factory
Singleton
check.explanation: Same interface in and out, with behavior added around each call, is a decorator. An adapter would change the interface to fit what the caller expects.

sections.title: Singleton and dependency injection
sections.key: Instead of a singleton that code reaches for globally, create one instance at startup and pass it in: dependency injection makes dependencies visible and tests easy.
sections.body:
A **singleton** guarantees one instance of a class with global access: `Config.instance()`, or in Python a module-level object everyone imports. It sounds tidy, but many reviewers treat a hand-rolled singleton as a smell.

[[visual]]

Wanting one instance is fine. Create it **once at startup and pass it to whoever needs it**. That is **dependency injection** (DI): an object receives its dependencies from outside, usually through its constructor.

The place that builds the real objects and wires them together is the **composition root**: `main()`, an app factory or the framework's startup. DI is just passing arguments; frameworks such as FastAPI (`Depends`), NestJS, Angular and Spring automate the wiring.

[[code]]

Python runs a module once per process and caches it, so module-level objects already act as singletons: `logging.getLogger("payments")` returns the same logger every time. Fine for logging; for business state or outside services, inject.

items.title: Singleton
points: Global state in disguise: any code can read and change it
Hides dependencies: `Database.instance()` inside a method is in no signature
State leaks between tests, so results depend on test order
Couples code to one concrete class

items.title: Dependency injection
points: Dependencies are visible in the constructor
Tests pass in fakes, with no patching
Swapping SQLite for Postgres, or one email provider for another, is one change

sections.pitfall: Replacing a singleton with a module-level instance that every function imports. It is the same hidden global state under another name. Pass the instance in instead.

check.question: Why is `ReportService(db)` easier to test than a ReportService that calls `Database.instance()` inside its methods?
choices: Constructors run faster than class methods
Singletons cannot be called from inside methods
A test can pass in a fake database directly, and the dependency is visible in the constructor
Dependency injection removes the need for a database
check.explanation: With injection the test controls the dependency: it builds a fake and hands it over. With the singleton, the test has to patch a global and remember to reset it, or state leaks into other tests.

sections.title: MVC, and using patterns wisely
sections.key: In MVC the model holds data and business rules, the view presents, and a thin controller connects them; add any pattern only when a real problem calls for it.
sections.body:
Many web frameworks organize an app as **MVC: model, view, controller**:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The names vary by framework:

[[visual 3]]

The rule that matters more than the names: **keep business rules in the model or a service layer, not in controllers or templates**. A thin controller parses input, calls one or two model methods and returns a response.

If "shipped orders cannot be cancelled" lives in a controller, the mobile API, admin tool and nightly job each reimplement it, and the copies drift.

**Use patterns wisely.** They are a shared vocabulary ("put an adapter around the old billing API"), not goals. Start with the simplest code that works. When a real force appears, such as a second implementation or a test that cannot reach a dependency, refactor toward the pattern. Name the problem first, the pattern second.

[[code]]

visual.title: MVC
rows: Model
Data and business rules
An `Order`, its total, "shipped orders cannot be cancelled"
View
Presentation only, no rules
An HTML template, a JSON serializer, a React component
Controller
Handles input
Receives the request, calls the model, chooses the view

steps.label: The router matches the URL to a controller action
The controller parses the request input
The model applies business rules and loads or saves data
The controller picks a view and passes it the data
The view renders HTML or JSON for the response

visual.title: Same roles, different names
rows: Rails, Laravel, Spring MVC, ASP.NET MVC
Controller
View
Django (MTV)
**View**
**Template**
Express
Route handler
Template or JSON
visual.caption: In Django a **view** does the controller's job and a **template** is the view.

sections.pitfall: Fat controllers: business rules written inside route handlers. Other entry points cannot reuse them and they are hard to unit test. Move the rule into the model or a service and keep the controller thin.

check.question: In Django's MTV naming, which piece plays the role that a controller plays in MVC?
choices: The model
The template
The view
The settings file
check.explanation: A Django view function or class receives the request, calls the models and picks a template to render, which is the controller's job. The template is what MVC calls the view.

keyTerms.definition: Single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
A subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected without breaking callers' assumptions.
Building behavior by holding other objects and delegating to them, a has-a relationship.
Interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen by the caller.
A function or method that centralizes the decision of which object to create.
A subject notifies subscribed listeners when something happens, without knowing what they do.
Publishers send to topics through a broker; subscribers read topics. Neither side knows the other.
A wrapper that translates one interface into the interface the client expects.
A wrapper with the same interface as the wrapped object that adds behavior such as logging or caching.
A class with exactly one globally accessible instance; often a smell because it hides global state.
Passing an object its collaborators from outside, usually through the constructor.
Model (data and rules), view (presentation), controller (handles input and coordinates).

summary: SOLID: one job, extend without editing, honest subclasses, small interfaces, depend on abstractions.
Favor composition; keep inheritance for true is-a relationships.
Strategy swaps algorithms behind one interface; a factory picks one in a single place.
Observer and pub/sub decouple triggers from reactions; always unsubscribe.
Adapters translate interfaces; decorators keep the interface and add behavior.
Prefer dependency injection to singletons, keep controllers thin, add patterns only when needed.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a fellow intern how you would design a notification feature that sends email, SMS and push messages, using composition, a strategy or two, a factory and dependency injection, and why you would avoid a singleton and a deep class hierarchy.

questions.question: Match each SOLID principle to the code that violates it.

pairs.right: An Invoice class that calculates totals, renders PDFs and emails customers
Adding a payment method means editing the same if chain in five functions
A subclass's save() raises NotImplementedError where callers expect it to work
A basic printer class is forced to implement scan() and fax()
SignupService constructs its own SmtpClient inside __init__

questions.explanation: Each principle names a specific way code becomes hard to change: too many jobs, edits instead of extensions, subclasses that break promises, bloated interfaces, and high-level code welded to low-level details.

questions.question: What does the open/closed principle ask for?
choices: Classes should be closed to subclassing
Add new behavior by adding code, without editing code that already works
Every attribute should be private
Files and connections should always be closed after use
questions.explanation: Open for extension, closed for modification: a new shape, payment type or export format should arrive as new code that plugs in, while tested code stays untouched.

questions.question: stretch() was written for rectangles and assumes set_width leaves the height alone. With a Square it returns 100 instead of 50. Which principle does Square break?
choices: Interface segregation: Square has too many methods
Single responsibility: Square does two jobs
Dependency inversion: stretch depends on a concrete class
Liskov substitution: Square cannot replace Rectangle without changing behavior callers rely on
questions.explanation: Mathematically a square is a rectangle, but behaviorally this Square breaks Rectangle's promise that width and height change independently. Code written for the parent silently gets wrong answers. Model them as separate shapes that share a Shape interface instead.

questions.question: Complete total_area so that adding a new shape class never requires editing it.
choices: area(shape)
shape.area
shape.area()
Circle.area(shape)
questions.explanation: Calling shape.area() lets each shape compute its own area, so a new Hexagon class just works. shape.area without parentheses is the method itself, not a number, and Circle.area(shape) only works for circles.

questions.question: A codebase has EmailNotifier, LoggedEmailNotifier, RetryingEmailNotifier and LoggedRetryingEmailNotifier, plus the same four for SMS. What is a better design?
choices: Add a third level of inheritance for push notifications
Merge all eight into one class with boolean flags
A Notifier that holds a list of channels plus optional logging and retry objects
Make every notifier a singleton
questions.explanation: Composition covers every combination by assembling small parts, so a new channel or behavior is one new class instead of a new row of subclasses. Boolean flags just move the explosion into if statements.

questions.question: Which of these is a good use of inheritance?
choices: OrderService extends DatabaseHelper to reuse its query method
InsufficientFundsError extends Exception
Car extends Engine because every car has an engine
Stack extends list to reuse append and pop
questions.explanation: An InsufficientFundsError really is an Exception and works everywhere one is expected. The others are has-a or code-reuse relationships: a car has an engine, a service uses a database helper, a stack uses a list internally.

questions.question: Give two reasons composition usually ages better than deep inheritance.
questions.answer: You can combine behaviors freely instead of writing a subclass for every combination, and objects depend only on their collaborators' public methods rather than a parent's internals, so changes ripple less and tests can pass in fakes.
questions.explanation: Inheritance is the tightest coupling a language offers. Composition keeps parts small and replaceable, which is what most future changes need.

questions.question: The subclass counts appends, but this prints 1 instead of 3. Why?
questions.code:
class CountingList(list):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.added = 0

    def append(self, item):
        self.added += 1
        super().append(item)

c = CountingList()
c.append("a")
c.extend(["b", "c"])
print(c.added)
choices: super().append runs before self.added is updated
list.extend does not call append, so the override is bypassed; the subclass silently depends on how the parent works inside
Instance attributes cannot be added to subclasses of list
extend builds a new list instead of changing c
questions.explanation: This is the fragile base class problem: the subclass's correctness depends on the parent's private implementation. A class that holds a list and exposes its own add and add_many methods controls every path and cannot be bypassed.

questions.question: Match each pattern to the problem it solves.

pairs.right: Swap the pricing algorithm per customer type without touching checkout
Decide in one place which notifier class to build from a config string
Let email, analytics and the dashboard react when an order ships
Make a vendor SDK fit your app's PaymentGateway interface
Add caching around a repository without changing its interface
Hand a service a fake clock in tests

questions.explanation: Strategy varies an algorithm, factory centralizes creation, observer broadcasts events, adapter translates interfaces, decorator adds behavior behind the same interface, and dependency injection supplies collaborators from outside.

questions.question: sort_products receives a strategy function. Complete the call so the caller's strategy decides the order.
choices: strategy()
"strategy"
by_price
strategy
questions.explanation: key expects a function to call on each item, so you pass the function object itself. strategy() calls it with no arguments and crashes, and hard-coding by_price ignores the caller's choice.

questions.question: Customers who pick "Express" (capital E) quietly get standard shipping, and complaints pile up. What is the design problem?
choices: Factories cannot use dictionaries
Classes cannot be stored as dictionary values
get() creates two instances of the class
The factory silently falls back for unknown names; normalize the input and raise a clear error for names it does not know
questions.explanation: A silent default hides a real mismatch between what the caller asked for and what exists. The factory is the one place that knows every valid option, so it should normalize (lowercase) and fail loudly otherwise.

questions.question: When is a plain function a better strategy than a strategy class in Python?
choices: When the strategy is one operation with no configuration or state
Never, because the pattern requires classes
Only when the strategy has more than three methods
When you need many instances with different settings and shared helpers
questions.explanation: Python functions are first-class objects, so a one-operation strategy is just a function, like the key passed to sorted(). Classes earn their keep when a strategy carries settings or several related methods.

questions.question: In the browser, `button.addEventListener('click', onClick)` is an example of which pattern?
choices: Singleton
Adapter
Observer
Factory
questions.explanation: The button is the subject and onClick is an observer that subscribed to its click events. The button does not know what the handler does, it just calls every listener.

questions.question: After the user opens the chat panel five times, every new message triggers render five times. What is wrong?
choices: Each call adds a new listener and none is ever removed; keep the unsubscribe function and call it when the panel closes
subscribe must be called before the panel object is created
Arrow functions cannot be used as listeners
The bus publishes each message once per subscriber name
questions.explanation: Old panels are gone from the screen, but their listeners still run and keep the panels in memory. Store what subscribe returns and call it on close, or subscribe once and reuse the panel.

questions.question: Which of these are real costs of the observer pattern?
choices: Reading the code that publishes an event does not show what will run
Listeners that are never removed keep firing and leak memory
In a naive loop, one listener that throws stops the listeners after it
The subject must know every observer's concrete class
Adding a new reaction requires editing the subject
questions.explanation: Decoupling has a price in traceability, cleanup and error handling. The last two are exactly what the pattern removes: the subject only knows the listener interface, and new reactions are new subscriptions.

questions.question: The order service publishes `order.shipped` to a Kafka topic, and the email and analytics services consume it. What does the order service know about those consumers?
choices: Each consumer's URL
Which consumer classes to instantiate
How many consumers handled the message before publish returns
Nothing beyond the topic it publishes to
questions.explanation: With a broker, the publisher only knows the topic. Consumers can be added, removed or restarted without any change to the order service, which is the point of pub/sub between services.

questions.question: Your code expects `get_user(id)` to return `{'username': ...}`. A legacy service offers `fetchUserRecord(id)` returning `{'user_name': ...}`. Which pattern fits?
choices: Adapter
Observer
Singleton
Strategy
questions.explanation: An adapter implements the interface your code expects (get_user returning username) and translates calls and field names to the legacy service, so neither side has to change.

questions.question: Complete the decorator so the wrapped function still runs and returns its result.
choices: wrapper(*args, **kwargs)
func(*args, **kwargs)
func
timed(func)
questions.explanation: The wrapper must call the original function with whatever arguments it received. Calling wrapper would recurse forever, plain func is the function object rather than its result, and timed(func) just builds another wrapper.

questions.question: This prints "calling add" and then None. Why?
choices: Decorators cannot wrap functions that take arguments
The print inside wrapper replaces the return value
wrapper calls func but never returns its result
@logged runs add before it is defined
questions.explanation: add(2, 3) now calls wrapper, which computes 5 and throws it away, so it returns None. A decorator must return func(*args, **kwargs) to keep the original contract. That is the same promise the decorator pattern makes: same interface, extra behavior.

questions.question: What is the key difference between an adapter and a decorator?
choices: An adapter adds behavior; a decorator converts one interface into another
Adapters only wrap classes; decorators only wrap functions
They are two names for the same pattern
An adapter changes the interface to the one the client expects; a decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior
questions.explanation: Both wrap another object. The adapter's job is translation between mismatched interfaces; the decorator's job is extra behavior such as logging or caching behind an unchanged interface, which is why decorators can be stacked.

questions.question: Why should a vendor SDK be wrapped in an adapter instead of being called directly throughout the app?
questions.answer: So the vendor's types and calls live in one place behind your own interface. Switching providers or absorbing an SDK change means editing one adapter, and tests can fake your small interface instead of the vendor's.
questions.explanation: Direct calls spread the vendor's shape into every file, so each change to the vendor becomes a change to your whole app.

questions.question: Which of these are common criticisms of the singleton pattern?
choices: It is global state that any code can read and change
Code that uses it hides the dependency instead of declaring it in a signature
Its state can leak between tests, making results depend on test order
It makes every object creation slower
It cannot be implemented in Python
questions.explanation: The problems are global mutable state, hidden coupling and test isolation. Performance is not the issue, and Python can express singletons easily, including through module-level objects.

questions.question: Complete the constructor so InvoiceService receives its collaborators through dependency injection.
choices: self
clock, mailer
Database.instance()
*args
questions.explanation: Declaring clock and mailer as parameters makes the dependencies explicit, and the test passes fakes for both. *args would leave clock and mailer undefined, and a method call is not valid parameter syntax.

questions.question: What is the composition root?
choices: The place, usually at startup, where the real objects are created and wired together
The base class every service inherits from
The first commit in the repository
A global registry that any code can ask for any dependency
questions.explanation: Wiring happens once, near main() or the app factory, and everything below it simply receives what it needs. A global registry that code queries from anywhere (a service locator) brings back the hidden dependencies DI was meant to remove.

questions.question: test_default_checkout passes alone but fails when run after test_new_checkout_enabled. Why?
choices: pytest runs tests in parallel by default
Class attributes are reset after each test, so _instance is lost
The singleton keeps its state between tests, so the flag enabled in the first test is still on
assert cannot compare integers returned by functions
questions.explanation: _instance lives on the class for the whole test run, so the set is shared. Inject a FeatureFlags object into checkout_version instead, and each test builds its own.

questions.question: Which Python standard-library function returns the same logger object every time you call it with the same name? Type its dotted name, without parentheses.
questions.explanation: logging keeps one logger per name for the whole process, which is why modules can each call logging.getLogger(__name__) and share configuration. It is a singleton-like registry that is acceptable for global plumbing like logging.

questions.question: Match each part of MVC to its job.

pairs.right: Holds data and business rules, such as "shipped orders cannot be cancelled"
Presents data as HTML, JSON or a UI component
Receives the request, calls the model and chooses the view

questions.explanation: Keeping the three apart means rules live in one place, presentation can change freely, and request handling stays thin.

questions.question: The admin tool and the mobile API implement refunds too, and their rules have drifted from this one. What is the design problem?
choices: The refund rule lives in a controller; move it into the Order model or a service so every entry point shares it
Express route handlers cannot be async
The response should be rendered with an HTML template
86_400_000 is not a valid number in TypeScript
questions.explanation: Business rules in a controller can only be reached through that one route, so every other entry point copies them. An order.refund(now) method that enforces the rule gives one source of truth and is easy to unit test.

questions.question: A teammate proposes an interface, an abstract factory and three classes for a CSV export that has one format and no plans for another. What is the best response?
choices: Approve it, since more patterns make code more maintainable
Ask for a singleton too, so there is only ever one exporter
Suggest a simple function now, and introducing the pattern when a second format actually appears
Ask for an observer as well, so other code can react to exports
questions.explanation: Patterns solve problems that exist. With one format there is nothing to vary, so the abstraction only adds indirection. When a second format arrives, refactoring a small function into a strategy is quick.

questions.question: Put the steps of a request through a typical MVC web app in order.
items: The router matches the URL to a controller action
The controller parses the request input
The model applies business rules and loads or saves data
The controller picks a view and passes it the data
The view renders HTML or JSON for the response
questions.explanation: Routing finds the controller, the controller translates input into calls on the model, and the result is handed to a view for presentation. Each layer has one kind of job.
